PAPER: Minds and Machines (2026) 36:6 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-025-09758-5 Artificial Creativity? Simona Chiodo1 Received: 14 February 2025 / Accepted: 24 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Can an artificial intelligence (AI), whose outputs are correlated with humans’ inputs in an extremely opaque way, be thought of as creative? I will answer in the nega- tive, starting with the analysis of the case of Edmond de Belamy, together with further cases. More precisely, I will offer the following three kinds of arguments. First, what results from testing the idea of creative AI against the background of traditional definitions of creativity, especially from a philosophical perspective. Sec- ond, what results from testing the idea of creative AI against the background of the notion of meta-sensemaking. Third, what results from testing the idea of creative AI against the background of the epistemology of creativity. After arguing that the pos- sible answer to my starting question is negative, at least in the sense that speaking of creative AI means speaking of something far different from human creativity, I will argue that the reflection upon the idea of creative AI should not make us lose sight of what is most important: what creativity is always for, i.e. making sense of our own existence, from art to anything, not only because it is a kind of existential urgency for us but also because it is pleasant in itself for us. Keywords Creativity · Artificial intelligence · Meta-sensemaking 1 Introduction In what follows, I will reflect upon the possible answer to the following question: can an artificial intelligence (AI), whose outputs are correlated with humans’ inputs in an extremely opaque way, be thought of as creative? My starting point is the assumption that speaking of creativity does not mean speaking of art. In Sect. 6, after argu- ing that the possible answer to my starting question is negative, at least in the sense that speaking of creative AI means speaking of something far different from human creativity, I will argue that the reflection upon the idea of creative AI should not make us lose sight of what is most important (which happens whenever we cannot see the wood for the trees): what creativity is always for—in other words, creativity always has a most important objective, of which we should not lose sight, no matter where we decide to extend its definition: making sense of our own existence, from art to anything, not only because it is a kind of existential urgency for us but also because it is pleasant in itself for us. 2 Creative AI? The exemplary case of Edmond de Belamy is promising when it comes to questioning the idea not only of artistic AI but also of creative AI. Edmond de Belamy is a portrait produced by an AI whose outputs opaquely correlate with humans’ inputs (and sold by Christie’s in 2018 for almost half a million dollars). The kind of AI used by Obvi- ous3 to produce Edmond de Belamy is generative, specifically generative adversarial networks (GANs), whose great autonomy is explained by Goodfellow, i.e. its inven- tor, through the following metaphor: [t]he basic idea of GANs is to set up a game between two players. One of them is called the generator. […] The other player is the discriminator. […] The generator is trained to fool the discriminator. We can think of the generator as being like a counterfeiter, trying to make fake money, and the discriminator as being like police, trying to allow legitimate money and catch counterfeit money. See also McCormack & d’Inverno, 2012, Veale & Cardoso, 2019, Anscomb, 2021 and Bown, 2021) Out of metaphor, the generator tries to produce AI images that the discriminator can- not distinguish from the human-made images on which it is trained. Specifically, Edmond de Belamy is an AI image that the discriminator cannot distinguish from the thousands of human-made portraits painted between the 14th and the 19th centuries on which it is trained. Importantly, Edmond de Belamy is an original image, in that it is neither a copy of the thousands of human-made portraits nor a collage of them nor an average of them. Conversely, it cannot fail to be an original image in the sense that it is (more directly) produced by the AI (i.e. the generator) that does not know the thousands of human- made portraits, and not by the AI (i.e. the discriminator) that knows them. Thus, even though Edmond de Belamy results from the system consisting of both the generator and the discriminator, there is a sense in which it is more directly produced by the former than by the latter. Even more importantly, Obvious attributes the word “creation” (Obvious, 2020, p. 168, my translation) to the AI: [d]oes it mean that an artist working with GAN algorithms makes no contribu- tion to the process in terms of inventiveness? No. It simply means that the artist focuses her creativity on other variables of the process or uses a different kind of creativity, and that the visual creation becomes more and more delegated to the tool. Some of the aspects on which the artist focuses are the choice of the theme, research related to the decision to treat this theme, the search for inspira- tion (which translates here into the search and choice of database components used as input for the algorithm), the programming and fine-tuning of the algo- rithm and the whole process based on trial and error, and the choice of means of expression. (Obvious, 2020, p. 168, my translation) The notion of “creativity” emerges in two cases: first, when it is attributed to a human process (“the artist focuses her creativity on other variables of the process”) and, second, when it is attributed to an artificial process (“the visual creation becomes more and more delegated to the tool”). If it is true that the former, i.e. human “cre- ativity”, is put into play in several cases (“the choice of the theme, research related to the decision to treat this theme, the search for inspiration […], the programming and fine-tuning of the algorithm and the whole process based on trial and error, and the choice of means of expression”), it is also true that, even if the latter, i.e. artificial “creativity”, is put into play in one case (“the visual creation”), the one case in which it is put into play is crucial. Indeed, “the visual creation” means the choice and reali- sation of the shaping itself that best represents the list of things attributed to human “creativity”—“the visual creation”, i.e. the shaping itself, means what is most crucial to the artefact itself according to most traditional definitions of creativity, as I will develop in the following section. In other words, I may be capable of choosing both “the theme” (for instance, human redemption) and the “means of expression” (for 1 3 6 Page 4 of 20 S. Chiodo instance, literature), but what most distinguishes me from Hugo is his unique capabil- ity to write Les Misérables—what most distinguishes creative humans is their unique capability to shape the artefact that best represents whatever “theme” others may be capable of choosing. Thus, it seems that speaking of an AI whose outputs opaquely correlate with humans’ inputs means speaking of the attribution of the most crucial creative act to an artificial process. Does it make sense? In what follows, I will reflect upon the possible attribution of creativity to an arti- ficial process, specifically AI’s, against the background of, first, traditional definitions of creativity, second, the notion of meta-sensemaking and, third, the epistemology of creativity. Again, I emphasise that I will reflect upon the issue of artificial creativity, and not of artificial artistry. 3 AI Against the Background of Traditional Definitions of Creativity Disruptive novel phenomena may make us think that traditional definitions are unser- viceable. For instance, AI, and especially generative AI, may make us think that the notion of creativity is to be revolutionised (see Moruzzi, 2022). Specifically, some- times we may happen to think that the notion of creativity is to be extended to the point that it can be applied to the case of Edmond de Belamy. And sometimes we may happen to think that the notion of creativity is to be dismissed. Yet, at least from a philosophical perspective, both options described above are not ideal, in that both lack analytical thinking. Conversely, analytical thinking offers at least the following two valuable opportunities: first, to better understand what we actually mean when we use the words “human creativity” (for instance, what does it mean to say that Hugo writing Les Misérables is creative when we say it against the background of the AI producing Edmond de Belamy?) and, second, to better understand what we actually mean when we use the words “artificial creativity” (for instance, what does it mean to say that the AI producing Edmond de Belamy is creative when we say it against the background of Hugo writing Les Misérables?). In other words, putting the words quoted above in tension offers the valuable opportunity to better understand both the past and the present through an increase, and not through a decrease, of meanings. Even though the notion of creativity has especially characterised Western culture of the last two centuries (see at least Tatarkiewicz, 1975 and Paul & Kaufman, 2014), in recent decades, it has pervaded both ordinary language and professional work, from philosophy to psychology. The literature review of the professional work on the notion of creativity is not the purpose of my article. Thus, in what follows, I will exclusively consider its cornerstones, and especially what matters most for the argu- ments I will develop. Interestingly enough, most scholars of the notion of creativity, from philosophers (on whom I will focus in what follows) to psychologists (see especially Amabile, 1996, Csíkszentmihályi, 1996, Mayer, 1999 and Runco, 2023), seem to share the following basic idea: speaking of creativity means speaking of the production of something that is not only novel but also valuable. As Gaut puts it in his literature review, “[t]here is a broad consensus that creativity is the capacity to produce things 1 3 Artificial Creativity? Page 5 of 20 6 that are original and valuable” (Gaut, 2010, 1039). More precisely, novelty (i.e. being “original”) means what is more obvious: I am creative if I can produce, for instance, a different glass from existing ones4. And value (i.e. being “valuable”) means what is less obvious: I am creative if I can produce, for instance, a better glass than existing ones—more precisely, I am creative if I can produce, for instance, a glass that sig- nificantly improves the quality of the drinking experience, as I will develop in what follows. Novelty and value are necessary and sufficient conditions for my production of the glass to be defined as creative. Conversely, I am not creative both if there is novelty without value (as in the case, for instance, of a rectangular glass, which fits neither the hand that holds it nor the mouth that drinks from it5) and if there is value without novelty (as in the case, for instance, of a glass copying an existing one). It is worth noting that the argument of the copresence of novelty and value arises from Kant’s philosophical work, according to which speaking of genius means speak- ing of both novelty, i.e. not “imitation” (Kant 1790, 5, 308), and value as “models, i.e. exemplary” artefacts (Kant 1790, 5, 308), which are far from being kinds of “original nonsense” (Kant 1790, 5, 308). Contemporary philosophers also emphasise the copresence of novelty and value when it comes to creativity (see, again, the literature review in Gaut, 2010, which I choose as one the clearest and most applicable). According to a philosopher inspired by Kant’s philosophical work, creativity is the capability to cross a kind of no man’s land extending from the universal rule (which is given) to its particular application (which is not given. See Garroni, 2010). Both novelty and value are at stake. The former is implied because the right ways of applying the rule are not given and the latter is implied because the rule is there (for instance, the glass is the artefact that fits both the hand that holds it and the mouth that drinks from it) to distinguish between its right applications (for instance, round glasses) from its wrong applications (for instance, rectangular glasses)—the rule is there to distinguish between its valuable applications from its non-valuable applications. If it is true that the production of something novel and valuable is key to creativity, it is also true that the process, i.e. the production itself of the artefact, is equally key (see at least Carruthers, 2006, Stokes, 2008 and Gaut, 2010)—creativity is the capa- bility of the producing agent. Consequently, creativity is further analysable as the kind of conditions that make the producing agent capable of it. Most scholars espe- cially focus on the following conditions, which are also capabilities: understanding, imagination and judgement (see especially Gaut, 2010, in addition to the following references). In the case of the glass, I am not cre- ative if I produce the right glass, i.e. novel and valuable, exclusively by accident (for instance, exclusively by accidentally breaking an existing glass). In the case of the glass, I am not creative if, for instance, I cannot judge the wrongness of the relationship between a particular rectangular glass and the universal rule according to which the glass is the artefact that fits both the hand that holds it and the mouth that drinks from it. Conversely, I am creative if, for instance, I can judge the rightness of the relationship between a particular round glass and the universal rule according to which the glass is the artefact that fits both the hand that holds it and the mouth that drinks from it. In recent decades, scholars have increasingly questioned the assumption that, if it is true that creativity is a capability of the producing agent that is further analysable as understanding, imagination and judgement, it is also true that it is exclusively human. According to Boden’s seminal works, “[t]here is no reason in principle why future AI models should not embody evaluative criteria powerful enough to allow them to transform their conceptual spaces in fruitfully creative (including H-creative [i.e. even from a historical perspective, see note 4]) ways” (Boden, 1998, 354. See also Boden, 1991 and 2009 and Boden & Edmonds, 2009), in that “[s]ome H-cre- ative ideas have already been generated by AI programmes, though usually by merely exploratory (or combinational) procedures. Interestingly enough, the reason why “AI originality is only just beginning” is its lack of something that partly overlaps with the conditions described above, specifically, first, “domain-expertise, which is required for mapping the conceptual space that is to be explored and/or transformed” (Boden, 1 3 Artificial Creativity? Thus, our question cannot fail to be if Edmond de Belamy can make us stop being “a very long way from that”. Before moving to a strictly theoretical reflection upon the possible answer to the question asked above, it is worth noting that the conditions described above, i.e. understanding, imagination and judgement underpinning creativity, may be thought of as what, from an etymological perspective, can exclusively characterise human processes—the capabilities underpinning creativity may be thought of as what, from an etymological perspective, cannot characterise artificial processes. Indeed, the English word “automation”, which by definition is what most charac- terises artificial processes, derives from the Greek word “αὐτοµατίζω” (transliterated as automatizo), which means to “act of oneself, act offhand or unadvisedly”7, “to be done spontaneously or at random”, “haphazard”, to “introduce the agency of chance”, “of things, [to] happen of themselves, casually”, “to be self-produced” and, “of natu- ral agencies, [to] act spontaneously”. Other Greek words sharing the identical etymo- logical root are meaningful, from “αὐτοµατισµός” (transliterated as automatismos), which means “that which happens of itself, chance”8, to “Αὐτοµατία” (transliterated as Automatia), which means “the goddess of chance”9, to “αὐτόµατον” (transliter- ated as automaton), which means “accident”10. Thus, the English word “automation”, which by definition is what most characterises artificial processes, means random- ness—from an etymological perspective, artificial processes are even the opposite of human processes, in that randomness, as what most characterises the former, is even the opposite of understanding, imagination and judgement, as what most char- acterises the latter, specifically as a set of typically autonomous capabilities. We may happen to think of both Les Misérables and Edmond de Belamy as artefacts that can discover, specifically make us discover, something novel and valuable. For instance, we may happen to think of the former as capable of discovering, specifically of making us discover, novel and valuable meanings of human redemption. And we may happen to think of the latter as capa- ble of discovering, specifically of making us discover, novel and valuable meanings of melancholy. Yet, Les Misérables and Edmond de Belamy are definitely different. The former, as produced by a human process, results from his autonomy, i.e. his autonomous capabilities of understanding, imagination and judgement—more pre- cisely, Les Misérables results from Hugo’s autonomous capability to write a (right) particular application (which is not given) of a universal rule (which is given as an idea of human redemption shared by most humans, according to which, for instance, human redemption is a matter of moving from the worst possible actions to the best possible actions). Thus, Hugo is creative and Les Misérables results from creativity. Conversely, the latter, as produced by an artificial process, results from its random- ness (in the sense I have specified above. See also note 11), i.e. its automated process of the thousands of human-made portraits painted between the 14th and the 19th centuries on which it is trained—more precisely, Edmond de Belamy results from the AI’s automated process of the statistical correlations between the starting data. Thus, the AI is not creative and Edmond de Belamy does not result from creativity: if it is true that it is capable of discovering, specifically of making us discover, novel and valuable meanings of melancholy, it is also, and especially, true that it does it randomly—indeed, the AI does not produce Edmond de Belamy in the way in which Hugo writes Les Misérables: the latter does it by understanding what human redemp- tion is, imagining what words make it better understood and judging their rightness, i.e. novelty and value, and the former does it randomly. More pre- cisely, it is not capable of the following operations, which define the notion of meta- sensemaking itself: 1. If the point argued above makes sense, what Edmond de Belamy lacks is artistry as the kind of profound meaning described above—Edmond de Belamy lacks artistry because it is an aesthetic shape without posterior and additional meaning, i.e. meta-sensemaking. In other words, my proposal is to think of Edmond de Belamy as we think of sunrises, sunsets and traffic lights. In front of both the former and the latter we may happen to discover novel and valuable meanings of something, from melancholy to the pas- sage of time. And, in both cases, the reason why we may happen to discover novel and valuable meanings is random in the following sense: both Edmond de Belamy and sunrises, sunsets and traffic lights may happen to make us discover novel and valuable meanings by being aesthetic shapes without posterior and additional mean- ings—if we happen to discover novel and valuable meanings, from melancholy to the passage of time, in front of both Edmond de Belamy and sunrises, sunsets and traffic lights, it is not because of their resulting from experiencing, reflecting upon and shap- ing the meanings of melancholy and the passage of time, but because of randomness, i.e. causes totally extraneous to meta-sensemaking, from the automated process of the statistical correlations between the starting data (which is totally extraneous to the meaning of melancholy) to the natural phenomenon of sunrises and sunsets (which is totally extraneous to the meaning of the passage of time) to the artificial production of traffic lights (which is totally extraneous to the meaning of the passage of time)12. Indeed, the artistry of Les Misérables also results from its capability to discover, specifically to make us discover, novel and valuable meanings of human redemption—in addition to its doing it not because of randomness, but because of Hugo’s capability to experience, reflect upon and shape what human redemption is. Thus, speaking of novelty and value means speaking of something that the notion of art and the notion of creativity share, even though the former meaningfully exceeds them and, conversely, the latter seems to coincide with them. If it makes sense, does it also mean that meta-sensemaking, which is key to the notion of art, is not key to the notion of creativity? More precisely, does it also mean that humans, and not AIs, can be artists, but both humans and AIs can be creative? Indeed, thinking of the notion of creativity against the background of the notion of meta-sensemaking may be instructive. Let us go back to the case of the glass, which can result from creativity if it is, for instance, a novel round glass with a diameter of 7 centimetres, which valuably fits both the hand and the mouth, as we have seen. Is meta-sensemaking key to the design of the glass described above? We may reason through the following logical steps: 1. Let us imagine that the glass described above is produced automatically, i.e. by an AI-driven 3D printer given the universal rule according to which the glass is the artefact that fits both the hand that holds it and the mouth that drinks from it. Indeed, the AI-driven 3D printer produces the novel round glass with the diam- eter of 7 centimetres, which valuably fits both the hand and the mouth. 2. And let us even imagine that the AI-driven 3D printer not only chooses the diam- eter of 7 centimetres (and not, for instance, of 6.9 and 7.1 centimetres) on the basis of millions of processed data on both human hands and mouths but also asserts: “The best glass is round and 7 centimetres in diameter. Trust me”. Is the AI-driven 3D printer creative? 3. Finally, let us imagine that, to answer the question asked above, we drink from the glass produced by the AI-driven 3D printer. Indeed, we seem to experience that it is both novel and valuable: it is even the best glass from which we have ever drunk. Again, is the AI-driven 3D printer creative? 4. My proposal is to answer that, even though it is the best glass from which we have ever drunk, it does not result from creativity, in that the AI-driven printer lacks what the millions of processed data cannot give it: it lacks what I propose to define as true abstraction and idealisation, of which I propose to think as what makes true value possible—and which has a close relationship with meta-sense- making (as I will develop in the following section). Let us start with novelty, which, according to my proposal, both the 3D-printed glass and Edmond de Belamy have. In the case of the 3D-printed glass, it is novel to the point that we can say that it is the best glass from which we have ever drunk, as we have seen. In the case of Edmond de Belamy, it is novel to the point that we can say that it is an original image, in that it is neither a copy of the thousands of human- made portraits nor a collage of them nor an average of them, as we have seen. Spe- cifically, it is not identical to any of the thousands of human-made portraits painted between the 14th and the 19th centuries on which the discriminator is trained. But, if we move from novelty to value, things seem to change. In the case of the 3D-printed glass, even though the AI-driven 3D printer asserts that “the best glass is round and 7 centimetres in diameter. Trust me”, we cannot actually trust it. Indeed, we cannot actually trust anyone but ourselves as humans who actually drink from the 3D-printed glass. By analogy, if I assert that “dark chocolate is better than milk chocolate” without ever having tasted either of them, you cannot actually trust me: indeed, you cannot actually trust anyone but yourselves as humans who have actu- ally tasted them both. In the case of Edmond de Belamy, even though in front of it we may happen to discover novel and valuable meanings of melancholy, there is a sense in which we cannot actually trust it: the meanings of melancholy we may happen to discover in front of it are valuable because of us, and not because of it—Edmond de Belamy does not result from understanding, imagining and judging what melancholy is, but from randomness. Indeed, we cannot actually trust anyone but ourselves as humans who actually feel what melancholy is. By analogy, let us imagine that a psychotherapist starts her career without ever having felt melancholy and ends her career having actually felt melancholy. And let us imagine that we want to start psy- chotherapy to cure our melancholy. At what stage in her life would we most trust the psychotherapist described above? The question asked above sounds almost rhetorical. And the reason why it sounds almost rhetorical is that there are experiences that far exceed the data, even though the data are millions—and, again, I propose to define what far exceeds the data as meta-sensemaking. If it makes sense, the point to emphasise is that there is a close relationship between meta-sensemaking and value—and, thus, there is a close relationship between meta- sensemaking and creativity as the capability to make not only something novel but also something valuable. If we think of creativity as the capability to find a right, i.e. novel and valuable, particular application (which is not given) of a universal rule (which is given), we may say that: 1. The psychotherapist who has actually felt melancholy is more likely to find a right, i.e. novel and valuable, particular psychotherapy to cure our melancholy, in that she can refine the data, i.e. what she studied in books, through something posterior and additional, i.e. her feeling what melancholy is. Indeed, it can make her realise almost instinctively, for instance, that the particular psychotherapy A, which is more standard and findable as exemplary in psychotherapy hand- books, does not work for us and, thus, that she has to try a kind of variant, i.e. the 1 3 6 Page 12 of 20 S. Chiodo particular psychotherapy B, which is less standard and not findable as exemplary in psychotherapy handbooks, for us. 2. You who have actually tasted varieties of chocolate are more likely to find a right, i.e. novel and valuable, particular combination of flavours to satisfy your taste, in that you can refine the data, i.e. what you read in cookbooks, through some- thing posterior and additional, i.e. your tasting what chocolate is. Indeed, it can make you realise almost instinctively, for instance, that the particular chocolate A, which is more standard and findable as exemplary in cookbooks, does not work for your particular combination of flavours and, thus, that you have to try a kind of variant, i.e. the particular chocolate B, which is less standard and not findable as exemplary in cookbooks, for your particular combination of flavours. 3. We who have actually drunk from the 3D-printed glass are more likely to find a right, i.e. novel and valuable, particular glass from which we drink better, in that we can refine the data, i.e. what the AI-driven 3D printer processed, through something posterior and additional, i.e. both our hands holding the glass and our mouths drinking from the glass. Indeed, it can make us realise almost instinc- tively, for instance, that the particular 3D-printed glass, which is more standard as the best choice of the AI-driven 3D printer, does not work for us, who hap- pened to drink from a curved leaf that inspired us, and, thus, that we have to try a kind of variant, i.e. the particular roundness inspired by the curved leaf, which is not standard to the point that it is not findable in the millions of processed data on both human hands and mouths. Yet, it turns out to be better for us. 4. And, if we move from the cases listed above to the case of Edmond de Belamy, things get even worse. Indeed, it would not be correct to say that we who have actually felt melancholy are more likely to find a right, i.e. novel and valuable, particular shape to represent our melancholy, in that we can refine the data, i.e. what the discriminator processed, through something posterior and additional, i.e. our feeling what melancholy is. And the reason why it would not be correct to say it is that there is no objective shared by us and the AI of Edmond de Belamy, whose particular shape does not have the objective of representing our melan- choly—again, there is a sense in which the meanings of melancholy we may happen to discover in front of Edmond de Belamy are valuable because of us, and not because of it. Indeed, in the case of Edmond de Belamy, value is unilateral, and not bilateral. On the one hand, we bring value, in the sense that we try to understand melancholy through a possible novel way of shaping it. On the other hand, the AI of Edmond de Belamy does not bring value, in the sense that it does not try to understand, specifically to make us understand, melancholy through a possible novel way of shaping it—again, there is a sense in which the meanings of melancholy we may happen to discover in front of Edmond de Belamy are random. 1 3 Artificial Creativity? Page 13 of 20 6 My proposal is to argue that, if there is randomness, there is no value13—and, if there is no value, there is no creativity as the capability to make not only something novel but also something valuable. Let us test the proposal argued above against the background of the following thought experiment. Let us imagine that the thousands of human-made portraits painted between the 14th and the 19th centuries on which the discriminator is trained are chosen by Obvious on the basis of the following criterion: they are right repre- sentations of melancholy. Would it be correct to say that Edmond de Belamy is not only novel but also valuable and, thus, that it results from creativity? My proposal is to answer that there would be a kind of randomness anyway and, thus, there would be no value anyway—and, thus, there would be no creativity anyway. In other words, what the AI of Edmond de Belamy would lack anyway is, again, meta-sensemak- ing as something posterior and additional to the data processed—again, the AI of Edmond de Belamy would lack our feeling what melancholy is—which can make us realise almost instinctively, for instance, that its particular shape does not work for us who can feel that melancholy is not only something that may be represented by dark colours and soft edges but also, and especially, something that may be represented by the right balance, which is exceedingly delicate, between a sense of bitterness and a sense of sweetness. And, even though the data processed are right representations of melancholy, it is hard to think of the AI of Edmond de Belamy as capable of choosing the right balance, which is exceedingly delicate, between a sense of bitterness and a sense of sweetness. But, if we imagine, in our thought experiment, that Edmond de Belamy can be both novel and valuable, in that it can represent melancholy through the right, i.e. exceedingly delicate, balance between a sense of bitterness and a sense of sweetness, it is hard to think of it as anything other than randomness. Again, the right choice does not result from meta-sensemaking as understanding, imagination and judgement, but from randomness as the way in which the AI can choose to shape Edmond de Belamy: not because it can find a valuable way of representing what it means to be melancholic, but because it can find a novel way of shaping something that it cannot distinguish from the processed data, and nothing more. Again, we can say that there is novelty, but we cannot say that there is value—which means, again, that we cannot say that there is creativity. The proposal argued above does not mean that randomness is exclusive to artifi- cial processes. Conversely, human processes can also make things randomly—and, if they make things randomly, they are not creative. Let us imagine that I scribble curved lines on a sheet of paper. And let us imagine that you are designers who want to create a novel and valuable glass and happen to see my scribbled curved lines. You exclaim: “Eureka!”. And you immediately draw something. Indeed, my scrib- bled curved lines make you find the right shape of the novel and valuable glass you want to create. Who among us is creative? My proposal is to answer that we are not both creative. More precisely, I am not creative and you are creative. And the reason why I am not creative is analogous to the reason why the AI of Edmond de Belamy is not creative: we both lack meta-sensemaking. The curved lines I scribble on a 13 At least in the sense in which I have used the word “value”, starting with the significant improvement of the quality of the human experience of something. 1 3 6 Page 14 of 20 S. Chiodo sheet of paper do not result from any (challenging) capability, starting with the (chal- lenging) capability to find a novel and valuable way of making a glass. Conversely, they result from nothing more than the (trivial) capability to scribble (random) lines. There is no meta-sensemaking as understanding, imagination and judgement in my action—again, there is no creativity in my action. Conversely, even though it is my scribbled curved lines that make you find the right shape of the novel and valuable glass you want to create, there is creativity in your action, i.e. immediate drawing, precisely because there is meta-sensemaking in your action: your capability to find the right shape of the novel and valuable glass you want to create inspired by what you see, starting with my scribbled curved lines, is challenging, and not trivial, pre- cisely because it means your challenging capabilities to understand, imagine and judge what its right shape may be. In other words, you can add something novel and valuable to what already exists, i.e. existing glasses. Conversely, I can add nothing more than scribbled curved lines to what already exists, i.e. existing glasses. And the reason why you draw creatively and I scribble non-creatively is, again, that your action is characterised by meta-sensemaking and my action is characterised by ran- domness—if there is randomness, and not meta-sensemaking, there is no creativity, no matter what the identity of the producing agent is. 5 AI Against the Background of the Epistemology of Creativity There is at least one further way of arguing that creativity requires meta-sensemaking which requires human processes: the reflection upon what we may define as the epis- temology of creativity. At least in Western culture, the epistemological functioning of creativity may be defined as a kind of culmination of the following three phases: first, analysis, second, abstraction and, third, idealisation14. Several philosophers work on them (see at least Brzeziński et al., 1990a and, 1990b, Coniglione, Poli and Rollinger, 2004 and Cart- wright and Jones, 2005). But their relationship with creativity is far less investigated (see at least Kieran 2018). Yet, there is a sense in which creativity may be thought of as the move from abstraction to idealisation. The first step is analysis anyway, which may be defined as the capability to identify what varies between things. For instance, if we consider the set of existing glasses, we are capable of analysing if we are capable of identifying their differences, from different shapes to different materials to different colours to any difference. After the exercise of analysis, we can move to the second step, i.e. abstraction, which may be defined as the capability to identify what does not vary between things. For instance, if we consider the set of existing glasses, we are capable of abstracting if we are capable of identifying their identicalities. More precisely, we are capable of abstracting if we are capable of answering the following question: after discarding the differences between existing glasses, from different shapes to different materi- als to different colours to any difference, what is left? A possible answer is what we 14 I worked on analysis, abstraction and idealisation as the typical Western ways of thinking (and creating) in Chiodo (2018). 1 3 Artificial Creativity? Page 15 of 20 6 have defined as the universal rule: the identicalities of existing glasses are, first, their being artefacts, second, their fitting the hands that hold them and, third, their fitting the mouths that drink from them. It is worth emphasising the intellectual refinement required by the exercise of abstraction, which Locke masterfully explains as follows: [i]n it [abstraction], an idea taken from a particular thing becomes a general representative of all of the same kind, and its name becomes a general name that is applicable to any existing thing that fits that abstract idea. […] Thus you observe the same colour today in chalk or snow that you yesterday saw in milk; your mind considers that appearance alone, makes it a representative of all of that kind, and gives it the name “whiteness”; and by that sound you signify the same quality, wherever it is imagined or met with. This is how universals, whether ideas or words, are made. (Locke 2008, II, 11, 9) Importantly, Locke specifies that abstraction, i.e. making “universals”, is not a matter of making something novel. For instance, when humans abstract the “universals” of being human after experiencing a variety of humans (from their parents to anyone), “they do not make anything new, but only leave out of the complex ideas they had of Nurse and Mamma, Peter and James, Mary and Jane, whatever is unique to each, and retain only what is common to them all” (Locke 1690, III, 3, 7). It is no coinci- dence that contemporary philosophers explain abstraction sometimes as “omitting of properties” (Nowak 1990, 193), i.e. the “properties” that vary from thing to thing, and sometimes as “omission of truth” (Jones, 2005, p. 175), i.e. what is discarded, even though it is true, in that, again, it varies from thing to thing. Even more importantly, specifying that abstraction is not a matter of making some- thing novel means specifying what most distinguishes it from idealisation. Indeed, after the exercise of abstraction, we can move to the third step, i.e. idealisation, which may be defined as the capability to change something true to improve it. For instance, if we consider the universal rule according to which glasses are, first, artefacts, sec- ond, that fit the hands that hold them and, third, that fit the mouths that drink from them, we are capable of idealising if we are capable of changing the universal rule resulting from our abstraction to improve both it and, consequently, the glasses we will make by applying it. More precisely, we are capable of idealising if we are capa- ble of answering the following question: after abstracting the universal rule of what existing glasses are, is there anything we can change, i.e. add, remove and modify, to improve both it and, consequently, the glasses we will make by applying it? A pos- sible answer is the following: we can add to the three sub-rules listed above the fourth sub-rule according to which glasses (also) fit the kinds of drinks they contain—which means a significant improvement of both the universal rule and, consequently, its applications, in that our change means significantly improving the quality of the rela- tionships not only between glasses and drinks (for instance, red wines will require larger glasses) but also between drinks and our drinking experiences (for instance, our drinking experiences of red wines will be tastier). It is worth emphasising the intellectual refinement required by the exercise of idealisation, which contemporary philosophers explain as follows: speaking of ide- 1 3 6 Page 16 of 20 S. Chiodo alisation means speaking of “misrepresentation” (Jones, 2005, p. 185), and even “assertion of a falsehood” (Jones, 2005, p. 175). Indeed, if we consider the set of existing glasses, what is likely to be “false” is that they fit the kinds of drinks they contain: it is likely that all of them are artefacts that fit both the hands that hold them and the mouths that drink from them, but it is not likely that all of them fit the kinds of drinks they contain. If it makes sense, we can go further and argue that there is a sense in which speak- ing of idealisation means speaking of creativity—more precisely, idealising means changing to improve, which means doing something novel and valuable, which means being creative. Even though idealisation (and, consequently, its relationship with creativity) espe- cially characterises Western culture (see at least Jullien, 2009), it may be promising precisely when it comes to reflecting upon creativity in Western culture. Thus, let us go back to the comparison between Les Misérables and Edmond de Belamy. We may reason through the following logical steps: 1. In the case of Les Misérables, it is possible to identify the kind of process described above, specifically idealisation. More precisely, it is possible to say that Hugo, no matter to what extent consciously and to what extent unconsciously, first, abstracts the “universals” of human redemption after experiencing a variety of it and, second, idealises by changing them to improve them—which means, again, doing something novel and valuable, which means, again, being creative. For instance, the significant improvement of both the “universals” of human redemp- tion and, consequently, its application, i.e. Les Misérables, may be thought of as the idea that human redemption (also) means sacrificing one’s own happiness for the happiness of others whenever circumstances require it. 2. In the case of Edmond de Belamy, it is not possible to identify the kind of process described above, specifically idealisation. Conversely, it is possible to identify the following kinds of processes: 2.1 In the case of Edmond de Belamy as it is, it is hard to even identify a kind of abstraction: indeed, there is a sense in which it is the generator (which does not know the thousands of human-made portraits), and not the discrimina- tor (which knows the thousands of human-made portraits), the AI that more directly produces Edmond de Belamy—which means that Edmond de Belamy is more directly produced by the AI that cannot abstract from anything. In other words, Edmond de Belamy is produced by trial and error, and not by abstraction: indeed, the generator tries “to fool the discriminator” by produc- ing “samples that are drawn from the same distribution as the training data”, which is far from trying to abstract the “universals” of something after expe- riencing a variety of it. 2.2 In the case of Edmond de Belamy as we have imagined it in our thought experiment (according to which the thousands of human-made portraits are chosen by Obvious as right representations of melancholy), it is equally hard to even identify a kind of abstraction: if it is true that there is a sense in which the AI that more directly produces Edmond de Belamy does not know the 1 3 Artificial Creativity? Page 17 of 20 6 thousands of human-made portraits, it is also true that Edmond de Belamy does not result from abstracting from right representations of melancholy. Again, Edmond de Belamy is produced by trial and error, and not by abstrac- tion. And, if it is true that there may be a way in which the discriminator, which is trained on right representations of melancholy, leads the generator to produce Edmond de Belamy as something that may make us reflect upon melancholy, it is also true that it would happen randomly—again, it would not happen by abstraction, but by trial and error that randomly make us reflect upon melancholy. By analogy, let us imagine the following case. I am a painter and you are a customer asking me to paint the portrait of your father. But I cannot know your father, in that he is dead. Thus, you bring me several photographs of him. My proposal is to argue that the portrait I can paint, if any, is worse than the portrait I could paint if I knew him. If it makes sense, the point to emphasise is, again, that there are experiences that far exceed the data, even though the data are millions—and, again, I propose to define what far exceeds the data as meta-sensemaking. In the case of Edmond de Belamy, there is no meta-sensemaking, no matter what the sub-case is, from (2.1) to (2.2) In the case of the portrait of your father, even though, at least potentially, there is the capability of meta-sensemaking (in that I can experience, reflect upon and shape what it means, in general, to be human), there is actually a weaker capability of meta- sensemaking, if any (in that, if I cannot know your father, I cannot experience, reflect upon and shape what it means, in particular, to be him, which is precisely what you ask me as my customer). If I knew your father, I could even paint the kind of portrait that may reveal something novel and valuable about him to you. It is hard to think that the AI can do it—and, if it does it, the cause of what it does is, again, random- ness, and not meta-sensemaking. Thus, the reflection upon what we may define as the epistemology of creativity seems to lead us to something analogous to what results from both traditional defini- tions of creativity and, and especially, meta-sensemaking: it is hard to think of AI as creative, in that what it lacks is especially value, i.e. what may be thought of as the move from abstraction to idealisation—which also means that what AI lacks is especially meta-sensemaking as closely related with both the former and the latter, as we have seen. In other words, we may argue that what AI lacks is especially being human, which means that there are (still) things that make sense if the processes are human, and do not make sense if the processes are artificial—there are (still) things that make sense precisely because of being human. 6 Conclusion Does it mean that we do not need AI when it comes to creativity? I would not answer in the affirmative. Both generative and non-generative AI can enhance our creativity by offering novel opportunities to generate value—which means, again, that novelty can result from both AI and us, but value can exclusively result from us. In other words, Edmond de Belamy can offer novel opportunities to generate valuable ways 1 3 6 Page 18 of 20 S. Chiodo of shaping melancholy, but the reasons for their value can exclusively result from our experience of melancholy as what can both generate and judge their rightness. Again, even traffic lights can offer novel opportunities to generate valuable ways of shaping melancholy (for instance, when they are stuck on red). But it makes no sense to think that the reasons for their value result from traffic lights, which are nothing more than randomly stuck on red—and Edmond de Belamy is far closer to traffic lights than to us, in that, again, it is nothing more than randomly characterised by dark colours and soft edges and, thus, evoking melancholy. The more general conclusion may be that we should not continuously compare AI with us. If it is true that the former may be a promising way of better understanding the latter, starting with the (mysterious) human mind (see at least Dartnall, 1994 and Hofstadter, 199515), it is also true that there are countless cases in which comparing them makes no sense—more precisely, there are countless cases in which putting them in competition makes no sense. Indeed, at the end of the day, what matters to us as humans is not only to experi- ence, reflect upon and shape what it means to be human to make sense of our own existence, but also to do it in a pleasant way. More precisely, what matters to us is also to make sense of our own existence because it is pleasant in itself, from artistic ways of doing it to other ways of doing it—which also means that, even in the unre- alistic case in which future developments of AI will be capable of meta-sensemaking, it is likely that we will continue to make sense of our own existence, from art to any- thing, not only because it is a kind of existential urgency for us but also because it is pleasant in itself for us, even though it is tough. JSON: Name: meta_sensemaking_generative Title: Augmenting generative image models with iterative human experiential meta-sensemaking signals to increase value-oriented creativity in generated artifacts Short Hypothesis: Integrating iterative human experiential meta-sensemaking signals into the training loop of a generative image model causes the model's outputs to be rated significantly higher on the value component of creativity than outputs from an otherwise identical model trained without those signals. Related Work: Prior work includes generative adversarial networks and other deep generative models for image synthesis, computational creativity systems that emphasize novelty-generation, and human-in-the-loop methods such as preference learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback. Existing evaluation frameworks emphasize novelty, diversity, and perceptual quality but provide weaker operationalization of 'value' or experiential meaning. Human-in-the-loop approaches have been used to steer stylistic or preference outcomes, but they typically target surface-level preferences or reward proxies rather than structured human experiential abstractions and idealisations. Work on representation alignment touches latent-space interpretability but does not systematically connect model internal structure to human meta-sensemaking processes. Limitations of current methods include emphasis on novelty over judged value, opaque links between training data and perceived meaning, lack of datasets that encode experiential/idealisation annotations, and evaluation pipelines that conflate novelty, quality, and value without isolating meta-sensemaking effects. Abstract: This project operationalizes 'meta-sensemaking'—human experiential abstraction and idealisation—as a structured augmentation to generative image model training and evaluates whether this augmentation increases the value component of perceived creativity. We construct a dataset of images paired with human experiential annotations and idealisation counterfactuals, and implement an iterative training pipeline that integrates these signals via preference fine-tuning and latent-space conditioning. The main contributions are: (1) a formal data representation for meta-sensemaking signals that encodes experiential descriptions, idealisation transforms, and evaluative judgments; (2) a training protocol to inject those signals into a generative model without sacrificing image quality; and (3) an evaluation suite that separates novelty from value using human ratings and representational-alignment metrics. Expected outcomes are measurable increases in human-rated value for generated images, demonstrable alignment between model latent structure and human experiential dimensions, and evidence that value improvements are not solely explained by standard novelty or quality metrics. Experiments: Datasets: (A) baseline portrait corpus composed of historical and contemporary portraits used for unconditional generation; (B) meta-sensemaking annotation corpus: for a subset of portraits collect structured human annotations (experiential descriptors, counterfactual idealisations, ranked evaluative judgments) from N=500 annotators producing M=10 annotations per image; (C) controlled ergonomics dataset for glass design with objective measurements and human preference ratings for complementary domain validation. Baselines: (1) unconditional GAN trained on (A) (vanilla baseline); (2) GAN fine-tuned with human preference labels (preference baseline); (3) GAN with representation regularizers for interpretability (representation baseline). Proposed models: (P1) latent conditioning using meta-sensemaking embeddings; (P2) iterative preference fine-tuning incorporating idealisation counterfactuals; (P3) combined conditioning + iterative fine-tuning. Metrics: human-rated value (Likert 1-7) and novelty (Likert 1-7) measured independently; creativity composite (value weighted); image quality metrics (FID), diversity metrics (LPIPS-based diversity), novelty measured by minimum perceptual distance to training set, representational alignment via representational similarity analysis (RSA) between model latent activations and annotation embedding space, and inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha). Experimental setup: train all models using identical architecture and compute budget (e.g., StyleGAN2-class architecture, matched training epochs). Sampling: generate 1,000 images per model; collect human ratings from at least 200 independent raters per model-output using pairwise and absolute rating protocols; perform ablations: (A) remove experiential descriptors, (B) remove idealisation counterfactuals, (C) single-shot annotation injection vs iterative loop. Statistical tests: pre-registered paired t-tests and ANOVA on human-rated value between baselines and proposed models, effect size reporting (Cohen's d), correction for multiple comparisons. Secondary analyses: correlation and partial correlation of value with FID, diversity, and novelty to verify independence. Cross-validation: repeat experiments on portrait and glass datasets to test domain transfer. Risk Factors and Limitations: Subjectivity and bias in human annotations and ratings, including cultural and demographic skew in experiential descriptors; high cost and time for collecting structured meta-sensemaking annotations at scale; difficulty in fully isolating 'value' from correlated factors such as image quality or novelty leading to ambiguous causal attribution; potential overfitting to annotator population reducing generalization to broader audiences; representation alignment metrics may be noisy and not uniquely interpretable; compute and storage requirements for iterative fine-tuning and multiple baselines may be large; domain specificity: methods validated on portrait and design datasets may not transfer to other creative domains; risk that injected signals change surface style without producing genuine idealisation-level conceptual shifts; ethical concerns if models internalize biased or harmful experiential associations.
